newsitem.title: FRANCE: Algiers bans cars to thwart bombers.
newsitem.headline: Algiers bans cars to thwart bombers.

text.p: Algeria on Wednesday imposed a traffic ban in the streets of its capital Algiers to try to thwart car bomb attacks blamed by the authorities on Moslem fundamentalists.
The 12-hour daily ban, from 7 a.m. to 7 p.m., is seen as the first move in a long-awaited strategy to counter a rash of bombings, mostly in Algiers, and massacres in isolated hamlets just outside.

Algerian newspapers on Wednesday said the latest killing took place overnight on Monday to Tuesday when suspected Moslem guerrillas massacred a family of nine by hacking off their heads in a hamlet south of Algiers.
In the capital, many of the three million residents welcomed the attempt to end the fear caused by bomb attacks.
"Walking in the streets near parked cars chilled you to the bone as most stationary vehicles were feared as lethal things," said one resident, speaking by telephone.
Other residents also said they welcomed the rules which Cherif Rahmani, special minister for the city, said was a "difficult and painful" decision taken for security, civic and environmental reasons.
The ban covers 37 main avenues and seven squares, including Colonel Amirouche Boulevard where a car bomb killed more than 40 people and wounded 300 wounded in January 1995.
More than 70 people have been killed by bombs in Algiers and nearby Blida and Boufarik, in the past three weeks.

"The ban is a mixed blessing. On the one hand it is good as it would lead to easier flowing traffic but on the other hand it will hamper our business here," said a shop owner in one of the main commercial areas, Larbi Ben Mehidi street.
Officials said Algiers had only six car parks with a total capacity of 4,500. Government offices and banks and major firms have their own parking spaces.
Most workers either cram into communal taxis or commute on trains and city buses, which have long been a nightmare form of travel, packed with people and often breaking down through overloading.

Many of the half-million cars which used to ply the streets daily converge on the capital from the country's 47 provinces as Algerians come to shop or sort out administrative problems and bureaucracy.
Under the rules, trucks and vehicles can get exemption to unload goods for shops only between 9 a.m and 11 a.m.
"This is not enough time because it would be hard to arrange unloading of goods," said one trader speaking by telephone from his shop.

One resident who toured the city for more than two hours on Wednesday said: "There were no more police in the streets to enforce the rules. Perhaps the authorities are watching how people behave at first and will move later after the end of (the Moslem fasting month of) Ramadan."
Another man, also speaking by telephone, said he saw more drivers queuing for parking in city car parks.
One driver told Algerian state-run radio: "I will drive around to look for a place to put my car. If it is difficult, as I'm afraid, I will put it in the parking place forever."
The authorities said fees for municipal vehicle parks will be reduced by 25 percent. But some parks managers told Algerian radio they had received no official notice on this.
About 60,000 people have been killed in Algeria's violence since early 1992 when the authorities cancelled a general election in which radical Islamists had taken a huge lead.
